title: ASVAB Coach question bank
note: Original ASVAB-style practice questions written to the official content areas (see build/blueprint.md). Not real ASVAB items.

ar-rate.name: Distance, rate, and time
what: Distance is how far you go.
Rate is how fast. Time is how long.
ar-rate.why: AR asks rate questions on almost every test.
example: A ship goes 20 miles each hour.
After 2 hours, it went 40 miles.
ar-rate.idea: Distance equals rate times time. D = R x T.
worked: A truck drives 50 miles per hour for 3 hours.

ar-work.name: Working together
what: Work problems ask how long a job takes.
Add how much each worker does in 1 hour.
ar-work.why: These are tricky. Many people miss them.
example: You wash half the car in an hour.
A friend washes the other half in that hour.
Together you finish in 1 hour.
ar-work.idea: Find the part of the job done in 1 hour. Then flip it.
worked: Pump A fills a tank in 2 hours. Pump B in 2 hours.
Step 1: Each hour, A does 1/2. B does 1/2.

ar-percent.name: Percents: sales, tax, tips
what: Percent means "out of 100".
25% means 25 out of 100.
ar-percent.why: Sales, tax, tips, and pay raises use percents.
example: A $10 meal. You tip 20%.
20% of 10 is 2. You pay $12.
ar-percent.idea: Change the percent to a decimal. Then multiply.

ar-interest.name: Simple interest
what: Interest is money paid for using money.
Simple interest: I = P x r x t.
ar-interest.why: Banks and loans use it. AR tests it often.
example: You save $100 at 10% a year.
After 1 year you earn $10.
ar-interest.idea: Interest = principal times rate times time.

ar-ratio.name: Ratios and proportions
what: A ratio compares two amounts.
3 to 5 means 3 parts and 5 parts.
ar-ratio.why: Recipes, maps, and mixes all use ratios.
example: 2 scoops of mix for 1 cup of water.
For 3 cups, use 6 scoops.
ar-ratio.idea: Add the parts. Find one part. Then multiply.
worked: Red to blue is 1 to 3. There are 20 cars.

ar-average.name: Averages
what: The average is the fair share.
Add them all. Divide by how many.
ar-average.why: Test scores and pay use averages.
example: Three friends have $2, $4, and $6.
Total $12. Share it 3 ways: $4 each.
ar-average.idea: Average = total divided by how many.

ar-units.name: Units and time
what: Units tell what you measure.
Hours, minutes, feet, inches, gallons.
ar-units.why: You must match units before you do math.
example: A movie is 2 hours.
2 x 60 = 120 minutes.
ar-units.idea: Change to the same unit first. 1 hour = 60 minutes. 1 foot = 12 inches.

ar-fractions.name: Fractions in word problems
what: A fraction is a part of a whole.
3/4 means 3 of 4 equal parts.
ar-fractions.why: Tanks, books, and pay often use fractions.
example: A pizza has 8 slices.
You eat 1/4 of it. That is 2 slices.
ar-fractions.idea: To find a fraction of a number: divide by the bottom. Times the top.

ar-money.name: Money and totals
what: Many AR problems are shopping math.
Find the cost of each part. Then add.
ar-money.why: This is the most common AR question.
example: 2 sodas at $1.50 each.
ar-money.idea: Multiply price by how many. Then add or subtract.
worked: 3 shirts at $8 each and a hat for $5.

ar-number.name: Number puzzles
what: Number puzzles describe a number in words.
Turn the words into math.
ar-number.why: They test clear thinking, not hard math.
example: Two numbers add to 10. They differ by 2.
The numbers are 6 and 4.
ar-number.idea: Write what you know. Use the middle or the sum.
worked: Three numbers in a row add to 30.

ar-geometry.name: Area and perimeter in word problems
what: Area is the space inside. Perimeter is the edge.
Area of a rectangle = length x width.
ar-geometry.why: Paint, carpet, and fences use these.
example: A rug is 3 feet by 2 feet.
Area: 3 x 2 = 6 square feet.
ar-geometry.idea: Area = length x width. Perimeter = add all sides.
worked: A room is 10 by 12 feet. Tile covers 20 square feet a box.

mk-equations.name: Solving equations
what: An equation is a balance.
Both sides must stay equal.
mk-equations.why: MK has many "solve for x" questions.
example: A scale has a box and 2 pounds on one side.
5 pounds on the other side.
The box must weigh 3 pounds.
mk-equations.idea: Undo the steps. Do the same thing to both sides.
worked: Step 2: Divide both sides by 2. x = 3.

mk-inequalities.name: Inequalities
what: An inequality uses < or >.
Solve it like an equation.
mk-inequalities.why: One rule trips people up. Know it.
example: You need more than $5 for lunch.
Any amount over 5 works.
mk-inequalities.idea: If you multiply or divide by a negative, FLIP the sign.

mk-systems.name: Two equations
what: Two equations, two unknowns.
Combine them to get one unknown.
mk-systems.why: Shows up a few times on MK.
example: Two shirts cost $30. One costs $10 more.
Prices: $20 and $10.
mk-systems.idea: Add or subtract the equations so one letter goes away.

mk-exponents.name: Exponents and roots
what: An exponent says how many times to multiply.
3^2 means 3 x 3 = 9.
mk-exponents.why: Exponents and square roots are common on MK.
example: A square room is 4 feet on a side.
4^2 = 16 square feet.
The square root of 16 is 4.
mk-exponents.idea: Same base: multiply means add powers. Divide means subtract powers.

mk-polynomials.name: Expanding and factoring
what: Expanding multiplies out the parentheses.
Factoring goes backward.
mk-polynomials.why: MK uses these on harder questions.
example: 5 boxes of (2 apples + 3 pears).
That is 10 apples + 15 pears.
mk-polynomials.idea: Multiply each term by each term (FOIL). To factor, find two numbers that multiply and add.
worked: Step 2: x times 4 plus 1 times x = 5x.

mk-quadratics.name: Quadratic equations
what: A quadratic has an x^2.
It often has two answers.
mk-quadratics.why: MK asks to solve or factor them.
example: Two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 5.
They are 2 and 3.
mk-quadratics.idea: Factor. Then set each part equal to zero.
worked: Step 1: Numbers that multiply to 10, add to -7: -2 and -5.

mk-functions.name: Plugging in values
what: f(x) is a rule. Put a number in. Get a number out.
example: A rule: double it, then add 1.
Put in 3. Get 7.
mk-functions.idea: Replace x with the number. Then follow order of operations.

mk-area-volume.name: Area, perimeter, volume
what: Area is flat space inside. Volume is space in 3D.
Each shape has a formula.
mk-area-volume.why: Geometry is a big part of MK.
example: A shoebox is 10 by 6 by 4 inches.
Volume: 10 x 6 x 4 = 240 cubic inches.
mk-area-volume.idea: Rectangle: L x W. Triangle: half of base x height. Circle: pi x r^2. Box: L x W x H.
worked: A triangle has base 8 and height 5.
Step 1: Area = 1/2 x base x height.

mk-triangles-angles.name: Angles and right triangles
what: A triangle has 180 degrees inside.
A straight line is 180 degrees.
Right triangles use a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
mk-triangles-angles.why: Angle and triangle questions are common.
example: A ladder against a wall makes a right triangle.
The ladder is the long side.
mk-triangles-angles.idea: Angles in a triangle add to 180. For a right triangle, a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
worked: Legs are 3 and 4. Find the long side.

mk-fractions.name: Fractions and decimals
what: Fractions and decimals both show parts.
0.5 is the same as 1/2.
mk-fractions.why: MK tests adding, dividing, and changing them.
example: Half a dollar is $0.50.
A quarter is $0.25, or 1/4.
mk-fractions.idea: To add: match the bottoms. To divide: flip the second and multiply.

mk-number.name: Number facts
what: Primes, factors, multiples, order of operations.
Median, rounding, absolute value.
mk-number.why: These are quick points if you know the rules.
example: 12 cookies can be split by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12.
Those are the factors of 12.
mk-number.idea: Order of operations: parentheses, exponents, times and divide, then plus and minus.

mk-slope.name: Slope and graphs
what: Slope is how steep a line is.
Rise over run.
mk-slope.why: Lines and points show up on MK.
example: A ramp goes up 1 foot for every 4 feet forward.
Slope = 1/4.
mk-slope.idea: Slope = change in y divided by change in x. In y = mx + b, m is the slope.

mk-probability.name: Probability and counting
what: Probability is the chance something happens.
Chance = good outcomes / all outcomes.
mk-probability.why: One or two MK questions use this.
example: A coin has 2 sides.
Chance of heads = 1/2.
mk-probability.idea: Count the good outcomes. Divide by all outcomes. For two events in a row, multiply.
worked: A bag has 2 red, 3 blue. Pick one.

wk-context.name: Word meaning in a sentence
what: You see a word in a sentence.
Pick the word that means the same.
wk-context.why: WK and PC make up VE. VE counts double for AFQT. It is in every IT line score.
example: "The soup was SCALDING. I burned my tongue."
The clue "burned" tells you: very hot.
wk-context.idea: Use the sentence as a clue. Is the mood good or bad?
worked: "The trail was ARDUOUS. We were tired."

wk-synonym.name: Word meaning (no sentence)
what: You see a word by itself.
Pick the word closest in meaning.
wk-synonym.why: About half the WK words come with no sentence.
example: MERRY means happy.
You can try "a merry day" in a sentence.
wk-synonym.idea: Make up your own short sentence with the word. Look for word parts.
worked: Step 1: Sentence: "Sleep is a benefit to health."
Step 3: BENEFIT means help or advantage.

pc-main-idea.name: Main idea
what: The main idea is what the whole passage is about.
It is the big point, not one detail.
pc-main-idea.why: Almost every PC set has a main idea question.
example: A text says: buy snacks, pick a movie, call friends.
The main idea: planning a movie night.
pc-main-idea.idea: Ask: what is the one big point? Check the first and last lines.
worked: Passage: "Dogs need walks. Dogs need food. Dogs need care."
Step 1: Every line is about caring for dogs.
Step 2: Main idea: dogs need care.

pc-detail.name: Finding details
what: A detail question asks for one fact.
The answer is written in the passage.
pc-detail.why: Detail questions are the easiest PC points.
example: A sign says: "Store opens at 9."
Q: When does it open? Find "9".
pc-detail.idea: Read the question first. Find the line that answers it.
worked: Passage: "The ship left at noon. It reached port at 6."
Q: When did it reach port?

pc-inference.name: Inference (reading between lines)
what: An inference is not said out loud.
You figure it out from clues.
pc-inference.why: Harder PC questions ask what you can infer.
example: Your friend comes in wet with an umbrella.
You infer it is raining.
pc-inference.idea: Pick the answer the passage supports. Do not add outside ideas.
worked: Passage: "Sam studied every day. He passed the test easily."

pc-vocab.name: Word meaning in a passage
what: Some PC questions ask what a word means.
The meaning comes from the passage.
pc-vocab.why: The common meaning may be a trap.
example: "The coach will FIELD questions."
Here FIELD means answer, not grass.
pc-vocab.idea: Put each choice in place of the word. Pick the one that fits.

pc-author.name: Author view, tone, and purpose
what: Tone is how the author feels.
Purpose is why the author wrote it.
pc-author.why: These test if you understand the writer.
example: A text says: "Wear a seat belt. It saves lives."
Purpose: to persuade you.
pc-author.idea: Look for feeling words. Ask: why did they write this?
worked: Passage: "Recycling is simple and helps us all."
Step 2: The author is in favor of recycling.

pc-sequence.name: Steps in order
what: Some passages give steps.
Words like first, next, then, finally show order.
example: First boil water. Next add noodles. Then drain.
Draining comes last.
pc-sequence.idea: Find the order words. Number the steps.
worked: "First save the file. Next close the app. Then restart."

gs-human-body.name: Human body
what: The body has systems.
Heart and blood, lungs, nerves, bones.
gs-human-body.why: GS often asks what each organ does.
example: After a run your heart beats fast.
It pumps more blood to your muscles.
gs-human-body.idea: Match each organ to its job.
worked: Q: Which organ helps you breathe?
Step 2: Air goes to the lungs.

gs-cells-life.name: Cells, plants, and living things
what: All living things are made of cells.
Plants make food from light.
gs-cells-life.why: Life science is a big part of GS.
example: A houseplant by a window grows toward the light.
It uses light to make food.
gs-cells-life.idea: Know the cell parts and how plants make food (photosynthesis).
worked: Q: What part of a cell makes energy?
Step 2: The mitochondria is the power plant.

gs-earth-space.name: Earth and space
what: Earth science covers rocks, weather, and planets.
gs-earth-space.why: A few GS questions each test.
example: Summer is warm because sunlight hits more directly.
That comes from the tilt of Earth.
gs-earth-space.idea: Know the planets in order, the rock types, and the layers of air.
worked: Step 1: The gas giants are big.

gs-chemistry.name: Matter and chemistry
what: Matter is anything with mass.
Atoms make up elements. Elements join into compounds.
gs-chemistry.why: GS asks about atoms, pH, and changes of state.
example: Ice melts into water. Same stuff, new form.
That is a physical change.
gs-chemistry.idea: Physical change: same stuff. Chemical change: new stuff. pH under 7 is acid.
worked: Q: Is burning wood a chemical change?
Step 1: Ash and smoke are new stuff.

gs-physics.name: Force, energy, heat, sound, light
what: Physics explains motion, energy, heat, sound, and light.
gs-physics.why: Physics also helps on EI and MC tests.
example: Pushing a cart: the harder you push, the faster it goes.
That is force.
gs-physics.idea: Know Newton's three laws and how heat moves: conduction, convection, radiation.
worked: Q: A pan handle gets hot on the stove. Why?

ei-basics.name: Current, voltage, resistance
what: Voltage is the push. Current is the flow.
Resistance slows the flow.
ei-basics.why: EI is in the main 4-year IT rule: AR + MK + EI + VE.
example: A garden hose: water pressure is voltage.
The water flow is current. A kink is resistance.
ei-basics.idea: Volts measure push. Amps measure flow. Ohms measure resistance. Kilo = 1,000. Milli = 1/1,000.

ei-ohms-law.name: Ohm's law
what: Ohm's law links volts, amps, and ohms.
V = I x R.
ei-ohms-law.why: Ohm's law questions show up on almost every EI test.
example: A 9 volt battery and a 3 ohm part.
9 divided by 3 = 3 amps of flow.
ei-ohms-law.idea: V = I x R. So I = V / R, and R = V / I.
worked: A 24 volt source and a 6 ohm resistor. Find the current.

ei-power.name: Electric power and energy
what: Power is how fast energy is used.
Power is measured in watts.
ei-power.why: Power and energy questions are quick EI points.
example: A 100 watt bulb uses more power than a 10 watt LED.
Run it 10 hours: 1,000 watt-hours = 1 kWh.
ei-power.idea: P = V x I. Also P = I x I x R. Energy = power x time.
worked: A 12 volt fan draws 3 amps. Find the power.

ei-series-parallel.name: Series and parallel circuits
what: Series: one path. Parallel: many paths.
ei-series-parallel.why: EI asks to add resistors and compare circuits.
example: Old holiday lights were in series. One bulb out, all out.
House outlets are in parallel. Each works alone.
ei-series-parallel.idea: Series: add the resistors. Parallel: product over sum. Two equal ones: divide by 2.
worked: A 6 ohm and a 12 ohm resistor in parallel.

ei-ac-dc.name: AC and DC
what: DC flows one way, like from a battery.
AC flips direction many times a second.
ei-ac-dc.why: Know which is which, and what hertz means.
example: A phone battery gives DC.
A wall outlet gives AC at 60 hertz.
ei-ac-dc.idea: AC = alternating current. DC = direct current. Hertz = cycles per second.
worked: Q: A car battery gives which kind?
Step 1: Batteries push current one way.

ei-components.name: Electronic parts
what: Each part has one main job.
Resistor limits. Capacitor stores charge. Diode is one-way.
ei-components.why: EI asks what each part does.
example: A fuse is like a safety valve.
Too much current melts it and stops the flow.
ei-components.idea: Resistor: limits current. Capacitor: stores charge. Diode: one way. Transistor: switch or amplifier. Transformer: changes AC voltage.
worked: Q: Which part changes AC to DC?
Step 1: AC to DC needs one-way flow.

ei-symbols-tools.name: Meters, symbols, and tools
what: Meters measure the circuit.
Schematics use symbols for parts.
ei-symbols-tools.why: Tools and symbols are an official EI area.
example: A voltmeter is like a pressure gauge.
It checks the push across a part.
ei-symbols-tools.idea: Ammeter: in series. Voltmeter: in parallel. Ohmmeter: resistance. Zigzag: resistor. Long and short lines: battery.
worked: Q: How do you hook up an ammeter?
Step 1: It measures flow through the wire.
Step 2: The current must pass through it.

ei-magnetism.name: Magnetism, motors, generators
what: Current makes a magnetic field.
A moving magnet can make current.
ei-magnetism.why: Motors, generators, relays, and transformers all use magnetism.
example: A fridge magnet sticks to the steel door.
Like poles push apart. Opposites pull.
ei-magnetism.idea: Like poles repel. Motor: electricity to motion. Generator: motion to electricity.
worked: Q: What does a generator do?
Step 3: It turns motion into electricity.

ei-materials.name: Conductors and insulators
what: Conductors let current flow. Insulators block it.
ei-materials.why: Safety and wiring questions use this.
example: Copper wire carries the current.
The plastic cover keeps it from shocking you.
ei-materials.idea: Metals conduct: silver, copper, gold, aluminum. Insulators: rubber, glass, plastic, dry wood. Silicon is a semiconductor.
worked: Q: Which is the best insulator: copper, iron, or glass?
Step 1: Copper and iron are metals.
